slides.title: Day 4 outcomes
body: Trace a message from producer to Delta.
Explain checkpoint restart and business event identity.
Validate, quarantine, monitor and document governance.
slides.notes: LO5 covers event ingestion, LO6 covers quality, observability and governance, and LO8 continues the project. You need evidence at the producer, broker/offset and output boundaries. The intentionally failed quality candidate is part of the correct experiment; your job is to show that it cannot replace approved data.

slides.title: Producer, broker and consumer
body: The producer sends a message.
Kafka stores records in a topic.
Spark consumes records and writes Delta.
slides.notes: A source NDJSON file makes the messages repeatable but is not a substitute for Kafka. The notebook uses a real producer and broker. A successful socket connection alone does not establish delivery. Inspect producer acknowledgments, consumer offsets and the resulting table records to connect the stages.

slides.title: Topics, partitions and offsets
body: A topic groups event records.
A partition provides an ordered sequence.
An offset identifies a record within its partition.
slides.notes: The lab uses two partitions and a trip-based message key. Ordering within a partition is not a total order across all topic records. Two partitions are not two replicas. This local one-broker experiment illustrates ingestion behavior without claiming multi-broker resilience.

slides.title: Streaming in a bounded lab
body: AvailableNow processes the currently available input.
Micro-batches commit results to the sink.
The query can stop after the available work finishes.
slides.notes: A bounded trigger lets you exercise a real streaming source in a classroom time window. It does not turn the broker into a file reader or simulate consumer results. The query uses the matching Spark Kafka connector and records progress. Inspect what the trigger consumed before proceeding to the next scenario.

slides.title: A checkpoint records progress
body: Keep the compatible source, destination and checkpoint.
Restarting the query can continue from recorded offsets.
A deleted broker is a different recovery problem.
slides.notes: Inside the same session, the experiment stops and restarts a compatible query while the source topic remains. Reusing a checkpoint after replacing the topic with an empty new one is not the same test. A fresh Colab VM requires a new Day 4 experiment from the Day 3 handoff, not a fabricated successful resume.

slides.title: Transport identity and event identity
body: Transport: topic, partition and offset.
Business: event_id and its approved payload.
Repeated delivery does not always mean a new observation.
slides.notes: Two separately sent records can have different offsets while carrying the same event. Producer idempotence handles a particular retry boundary; it does not remove every deliberate repeated send. The application must also inspect duplicate event IDs and reject conflicting content rather than silently selecting one version.

slides.title: Event time and arrival time
body: event_ts describes when the observation happened.
Ingestion metadata describes pipeline receipt.
Late and invalid are separate conditions.
slides.notes: An older timestamp with a new event ID can be valid late data. Missing IDs, impossible coordinates or unknown trips are different defects. State which clock a freshness measure uses. The supplied exercise materializes distinct events from a completed raw snapshot; it does not demonstrate a watermark-based state eviction policy.

slides.title: Quick activity: make the decision
body: Two Kafka messages have different offsets but the same event_id and identical payloads. How many deliveries and business events do they represent?
Think: 1 minute. Compare: 2 minutes. Discuss: 2 minutes.
slides.notes: Use the project terms rather than naming tools without a reason. State your choice and the assumption behind it. The activity is part of the explanation time and has no separate project mark.

slides.title: Activity answer
body: They represent two deliveries and one distinct business event. Transport offsets identify records in a partition; event_id identifies the business event.
slides.notes: Compare the reasoning as well as the final choice. If you selected another answer, identify which meaning of a row, time boundary or business rule led to it. The project will provide an observable example of this decision.

slides.title: Four streaming phases
body: Base and clean restart: 216 receipts, 216 events.
Two replayed messages: 218 receipts, 216 events.
One late new event: 219 receipts, 217 events.
slides.notes: Query identity persists during the compatible restart while the execution identity changes. The two explicit replayed messages become new transport positions but not new observations. The late event adds a new ID. Keep the original Day 1 GPS table and Day 4 stream receipt table separate so they are not accidentally counted together.

slides.title: A quality contract
body: Check required fields, keys and relationships.
Check values using the correct units and bounds.
Check whole-candidate completeness as well as individual rows.
slides.notes: A schema-correct snapshot can still have missing trips, duplicates or invalid values. Sixty individually valid rows would be incomplete for the 75-trip fixture. The quality policy defines both row rules and candidate-level checks. A fixed teaching threshold is not an automatically valid production SLA.

slides.title: Great Expectations in the project
body: Expectations express testable assertions.
A Suite groups expectations.
A GX Checkpoint runs validations and actions.
slides.notes: A GX Checkpoint is different from Spark's streaming checkpoint. The exercise validates a bounded Pandas snapshot collected from actual Delta data, then retains validation results and Data Docs. Great Expectations does not automatically repair values or quarantine rows; the surrounding application performs those actions using explicit reasons.

slides.title: Reject, quarantine, revalidate
body: Reject the 82-row mixed candidate.
Quarantine seven defective rows with reasons.
Validate a new 75-row candidate before approval.
slides.notes: The safe response to a failed whole-candidate check is to block its promotion. After separating invalid rows, run the quality rules again on the clean candidate. Do not assume that removing seven rows is enough. Preserve the original approved table and show which new candidate became eligible for downstream use.

slides.title: Operational observations
body: Volume: did you receive the expected population?
Freshness: which clock and reference time are compared?
Run health: where did processing succeed or stop?
slides.notes: A run can be technically successful while serving stale or incomplete data. The exercise uses fixed scenario times so the comparison remains reproducible. Distinguish old event time from recent delivery time. Record the measured value, its denominator or baseline, and the action the threshold would trigger.

slides.title: Governance decisions you can explain
body: Purpose and owner: why the product exists and who decides.
Lineage and access: where values came from and who may use them.
Retention: what you keep, where and for how long.
slides.notes: Use synthetic data only. In GOVERNANCE.md, separate implemented technical checks from proposed organizational controls. A folder label is not an authorization mechanism, and a local lab pass is not a compliance certification. Keep public source/evidence separate from private attendance, identity and grading records.

slides.title: Your end-of-lab question
body: A candidate contains 82 rows and fails because seven are invalid. How can you safely use the other 75?
Record your first answer and observed evidence in student/day04/REFLECTION.md.
slides.notes: Work from your own run before reading the next slide. State the relevant grain, identity or time boundary. A count, fare, validation field or short query result can support your explanation. This reflection contributes one point to the 100-point project.

slides.title: Model answer
body: Block the failed candidate, quarantine the seven rows with reasons, create a clean 75-row candidate, and run the quality gate again before approving it.
